Thank you, Your Excellency, for those remarks, and thank you for your leadership on this and your support for this mission. It is much appreciated. I will move back to an established speakers list. Next, I call on His Excellency Ito Bizon Ohaza, the Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Excellencies. I'd like to thank Canada for convening this meeting and its leadership of this group. This is the first time that I intervene as a Minister of Foreign Relations of my country, and I'd like to reaffirm the Dominican position of continuing to support and strengthen our relationship with Haiti. Haiti today needs for security, the institutional recovery, and development to move forward together. That is precisely the value these groups brings to help put the immediate response so that Haiti could recover its stability and build sustainable solutions. There has been some advances in security, but it's still frail and The force does not have enough contingencies as its mandate requires. On July 8th, its military component had 1,083 people, while the authorization was 5,550. It will not have full operational capacity until the last semester of this year. While this gap perseveres, we will still have the risk of losing what we've gained. This is why our priority should be clear. We need to full its commitment and give it its necessary resources for fulfilling its mandate. Security in itself will not resolve the Haitian crisis. This group has a big responsibility. Its contribution should help mobilize resources to strengthen the justice systems, support reintegration, recovery services, and generate economic opportunities. These are the conditions that would allow for the security gains to be sustained. We must also think what happens after each security gain. Each detention needs a justice system that can actually process them. Each young person that leaves a gang needs a real alternative. Each space that we've recovered must be translated in institutional presence, services, and opportunities. Security and development must move forward together and not one after the other. Haiti needs an economy that can generate jobs and offers opportunities to its young people, especially. The experience of the textile sector and the free zone can show that productive investment can contribute to these goals even under very difficult circumstances. The international community could help widen opportunities through financing, cooperation, and mechanisms to decrease the risk for productive investment. This area is an area in which ECOSOC and financial institutions, international financial institutions, and the UN system could contribute concretely. But this mustn't allow us to forget this is an emergency. Excellencies, Haiti needs to recover its security in order to recover its institutions and move forward towards free, credible, and inclusive elections. The Provisional Electoral Council has set December 13 for the first presidential run and 21st February 2027 for the second. The council itself has already set that calendar and said it depends on the acceptable security environment and the necessary financial resources for the elections to be carried out. The main responsibility is, of course, Haitian, but we need to support them. comprehensively with resources and political will. We mustn't allow this opportunity to be lost once again. Haiti does not need us to promise a future. What it needs is for us to support them to gain the present. Thank you so much.

Thank you, Excellency.

To His Excellency Carlos Ramiro Martinez, the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Guatemala. Sir, the floor is yours.

Good morning and welcome. From the time that we joined this group in 2024, Guatemala has taken this membership with a specific expression of its commitment to the Haitian people. We'd like to thank Canada for its leadership and efforts to keep Haiti as a priority in the international agenda. We believe the group plays a fundamental role to promote an international response that is coordinated to meet the immediate needs of the Haitian people and to also tackle the structural causes of this crisis through a comprehensive focus on security, institutional reinforcement, economic assistance, and sustainable development. These efforts must support the solutions led and taken on by the Haitians. The Guatemala's commitment is also seen in specific actions on the field. Currently, we have 150 military police in Haiti, and we will also add another 300 soon. To reestablish sustainable security conditions, it's necessary to strengthen Haitian institutions and generate the necessary conditions towards free, credible, and inclusive elections. We welcome the plans of the Prime Minister to carry them out and know what the government is doing to establish the proper situations. Guatemala will work with Haiti and Canada and the members of these groups and the UN system in order to promote international support, sustainable, coordinated, and according to the priorities of the Haitian people. Thank you very much.
Gracias.
Thank you.
I now turn to Her Excellency, Camina Johnson-Smith, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade for Jamaica.

Mr. Prime Minister, DSG, Excellencies, Jamaica remains deeply concerned by the multidimensional nature of the crisis in Haiti, which continues to have profound humanitarian, security, political, and socioeconomic consequences for the Haitian people and for the wider Caribbean. We therefore thank the organizers of this meeting, which provides an important opportunity for us to reaffirm the indispensable link between security, stability, and the economic development of Haiti. We join with the CARICOM statement delivered by the Bahamas. As you have heard, gains have been made, but the security climate remains tenuous. It is expected that as additional personnel are deployed, the GSF will continue to ramp up its efforts to assist the HNP and the Haitian armed forces to restore order in order for credible elections to be held in the first instance and more broadly. But as Haiti prepares for the first phase of its elections, a significant improvement in the security environment will be necessary to create the conditions for a credible, inclusive, and peaceful process. This reinforces the need for continued international backing for the GSF and its work in partnership with the HNP and the Haitian Armed Forces. In that light, Jamaica adds its voice to those who call on the Security Council members and on countries that have strong relations with them to support the renewal of the mandate of the GSF and for adequate resources to be allocated to expand and sustain the force's operations. A gap in GSF operations at this time will redound only to the benefit of the gangs and should absolutely not be allowed. Jamaica has contributed personnel to the GSF and is a member of the standing group of partners supporting it. We're providing command support and are training members of the GSF to ensure operational effectiveness, but so much more is required. Countries still ask how they can help. Financial support, troop contributions, logistics support, especially airlift for deployments, air and sea monitoring support are all critical needs. They are the specific ways in which members of the international community can provide support. There are countries willing to deploy, but which don't have airlift. There are countries with personnel able to provide intelligence support, but do not have the software. They require equipment on the ground. And there are countries with naval and coast guard personnel who could be deployed, but would require vessels. So funds, airlift, equipment, these would allow for exponential expansion in operational effectiveness. The plans are there, we need the people and the equipment to do the job. As you have heard, the JSF should be understood as a part of a broader Haitian-led response. And Jamaica firmly believes that the Haitian authorities and stakeholders must remain and do remain at the center of decisions concerning their political transition, security, recovery, and long-term development. At the same time, the international community has an important responsibility to strategically support these Haitian-led efforts, including by strengthening national and local capacities and helping to mobilize the resources required to implement their nationally determined priorities, as you have heard. Security gains are, however, indispensable to help create the space for political transition, restoration of state authority, and recovery. This is the reality. Security is a necessary precondition and parallel requirement for progress in all other areas. So let us move beyond words to actively support Haiti at this critical juncture in the ways they have already told us they need. I thank you.

Thank you, Excellency. We now take a moment to allow the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State, and the DSG to depart us for other commitments. Thank you. And thanks to all of you for your interventions today. I will move back to the established speakers list and remind again to please stick to the two-minute intervention limit. I now call on Her Excellency Hajja Labib, who is the Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management for the European Union. Excellency.

Excellencies, in Haiti today, childhood is being stolen. Children are being recruited by gangs. Families are trapped behind walls of violence. Humanitarian workers risk their lives to reach people in need. But Haiti is not alone. Europe stands with the Haitian people, with one goal: to help Haitians take back their future. Since 1994, the European Union has provided close to 600 million euros in humanitarian aid to Haiti, making it the largest recipient of EU humanitarian assistance in Latin America and the Caribbean. This year alone, our support amounts to 23 million euros. Our support helps survivors of gender-based violence. It keeps humanitarian flights moving, bringing vital supplies to hard-to-reach communities. We are also contributing to security with 10 million euros in support for the Haitian National Police and the Gang Suppression Force. Let me briefly focus on three things. First, security and human rights must go hand in hand. Humanitarian organizations must be able to reach communities safely. Aid workers must be protected, and the line between security operations and humanitarian action must remain clear. Second, children recruited by gangs are not targets. They are victims. In just the past year, three times as many children have been pulled into gangs. They need protection, they need a way out of violence and back into school. We must give them back their future. And that is why our humanitarian support is already funding educational projects. In a crisis, a classroom is more than a place to learn. It's a place of safety and hope. And third, Haiti needs more than a security response. Security is essential, but it must be matched by more humanitarian support that saves lives today and developments that gives people hope for future. Dear friends, now the international community must step up. Haiti's future cannot depend on emergency aid or the goodwill of donors. Haitians deserve the life to live in safety and dignity, to build their own future. And Europe will stand with them every step of the way. Thank you.

I thank the representative of the EU for her statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, His Excellency Dwight Fitzgerald Bramble, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Trade, Foreign Investment and Diaspora Affairs.

Thank you, Chair. My delegation aligns itself with the statement delivered by the Bahamas on behalf of CARICOM. Let me also thank you for your continued leadership of the ad hoc advisory group on Haiti and for ensuring that Haiti receives the international attention it needs. The ongoing crisis in Haiti, marked by unrelenting gang violence, mass displacement, food insecurity, and institutional fragility, demands a collective and coordinated response. We must sustain the security gains now underway, while above all, safeguarding the lives and livelihoods of the Haitian people. The deployment of the Gang Suppression Force is a welcomed and necessary step, and my delegation commends all those who worked to bring it into being. But the violence over the past year makes clear that force alone will not resolve this crisis. The Haitian National Police needs sustained support from all Member States and key partners, not only to confront armed gangs directly, but to help dismantle the financial and political networks that sustain them. Chair, food insecurity remains one of the most alarming dimensions of this crisis. With 5.7 million Haitians facing acute food insecurity this year, it is not only a humanitarian concern, but a matter of stability. International partners must continue to invest in strengthening Haitian institutions, governance, and national capacity so Haiti can deliver essential public services, safeguard the rule of law, address the root causes of violence, and lead its own path toward credible elections, sustainable development, and democratic governance. We urge all partners to increase funding for the humanitarian response plan, which currently receives less than 20% of the required amount. The catch-22 of the Haitian crisis is not merely that the political, security, and humanitarian dimensions demand urgent attention, but that they all demand equal, simultaneous attention. Advancing one track while neglecting the others has never proven sustainable, and risk unraveling progress made elsewhere. This is especially true as Haiti approaches this year's elections. A vote held amid unresolved insecurity and political criminal ties left unaddressed will not deliver the renewal it is meant to represent. We owe the Haitian people more than a vote in name only. Excellencies, fatigue cannot be an excuse for inaction. especially when lives hang in the balance and an entire nation's future is at stake. Let our conscience be our guide. The Haitian people have not given up. Neither should we. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Saint Vincent for his intervention, and I now turn the floor to Qatar, Dr. Mohammed Al-Khalaifi, the Minister of State for Foreign Affairs.

Thank you, Chair, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. At the outset, we would like to thank Canada for convening this important meeting. We also would like to express our gratitude for His Excellency, the Prime Minister of Haiti, for his insightful and powerful remarks. The State of Qatar reaffirms its steadfast commitment to the security, stability, and prosperity of Haiti as part of our mandate to contribute positively to the pathway of global peace and security. The situation in Haiti is of great importance, not for the region only, but also for the global peace and security. We remain deeply concerned by the multidimensional crisis facing the Haitian people and share the conviction that the pathway forward must be Haitian-led, with international communities playing a coordinated and sustained supporting role. The establishment of the GSF offers a cautious hope that security's conditions may improve. In support of this, of its mandate, the state of Qatar is proud that it has pledged previously a voluntarily contribution of a 30 million US dollars to the United Nation, uh, Trust Fund. Furthermore, the State of Qatar is honored to have joined the advisory board of the trust fund, and we look forward to the broad support of the renewal of the force mandate at the Security Council, uh, on the engagement with our, with the friendly people of, of Haiti, uh, Qatar has a long standing relationship. with its people. Between 2014 and 2024, Qatar Funds for Development supported education projects in coordination with Education Above All Foundation, as well as scholarship programs with several Qatari universities, totaling over $19 million. The State of Qatar will continue to stand with Haiti and its pathway to stability, recovery, and sustainable development. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the representative of Qatar for his statement, and I now give the floor to the United States of America, His Excellency Mike Waltz.

I thank you, Canada, for convening this important meeting. Colleagues, for decades, the international community has painfully watched Haiti suffer through cycle of violence, cycles of crisis after crisis. In fact, six different, six different UN missions have come and gone over the past 30 years. Billions of dollars have been spent, many by friends of Haiti, many by the countries in this very room, and we have to ask ourselves for what? Valiant efforts, absolutely. Well-intended efforts, most of them, to be sure. But we now have a situation where, despite those efforts, the Haitian institutions have gotten weaker, gangs have gotten stronger. Everyday people in Haiti, even in the region, even in our own countries, have paid the price. Last year, however, thanks to some rare unity in the Security Council, We decided to stop repeating the same mistakes and try something new. We built a new model. And through Security Council Resolution 2793, the Council created the Gang Suppression Force with a very clear mission: go on offense, after the gangs terrorizing the Haitian people. We then put a UN support office behind it to provide the logistics necessary to keep that force in the field. A group of regional countries banded together and joined forces to answer Haiti's call for help. The standing group of partners, as we call it, provides strategic direction, force generation, helps the GSF get the resources it needs. And colleagues, we've started a little bit of a new initiative, or call it Munga, Make the UN Great Again. I often feel like I'm saying it over and over again, but I believe it, and this is a place that needs to get back to basics. And this is one example of, I think, how the UN can become relevant and focused and create a difference for the people that it was created to help. So, colleagues, I'm happy to report that a good number of countries have responded by putting actions behind their words. We've received more than 17,000 personnel pledges for the 5,500 authorized billets. Think about that for a moment. We have more than three times as many personnel pledged as positions available. We now have 1,200 troops on the ground as we speak, 2,500 slated to be there within months towards that 5,500 authorization. I want to particularly thank Chad, El Salvador, Jamaica, Guatemala, Sri Lanka, the Dominican Republic, and I -- it's not a comprehensive list. There are many other countries putting soldiers and capabilities behind this mission. I also want to thank Germany in particular. We -- they answered our very recent call on strategic airlift that was so badly needed to get these troops and their equipment into Haiti faster, because, as we've all stated today, the people desperately need their help. And colleagues, I just want to talk about where the GSF has evolved over the last year. This was literally this time last year, a concept that we were negotiating in the council. Now here we are a year later. I was able to go visit just a few months ago. We have a Mongolian commander and his team on the ground. I have to say, as a former soldier, this team is the real deal. They are focused, they're planning, and they are moving forward with clearing roads that are blocked and used as toll collection mechanisms by the gangs. It's how they raise money. They're dismantling their revenue sources, and they're securing, once again, critical infrastructure that the people need to live their everyday lives. like the port in Port-au-Prince, the airport that has been shut down now for years, electricity and other key areas. So now we need to support this force and give them the people, the equipment, the resources they need to sustain it. Look, I have to say, as pleased as we were with the pledges, we need all of the countries to follow through with these pledges, as pleased as we are with the pledges to the trust fund, We need those checks to actually come in. Now, just to update those in the room, we are in the midst of negotiating the renewal on the Security Council, the mandate renewal, and we cannot find ourselves having spent the last year building this force up to put that mandate renewal in any type of jeopardy. The Council knew exactly what it was authorizing last year. With Resolution 2793, now is not the time to retreat from that decision. We cannot allow Haiti's security and the region's stability to become leverage in some unrelated geopolitical fights or conflicts or disputes that have nothing to do with the security of the Haitian people. Last year, to be candid, there were those who broke silence during these negotiations, but ultimately, ultimately did not object to moving forward with the gang suppression force. And we hope that position, that position must continue. We need to let it get to work because colleagues, while we debate words on paper here, The gangs are not stopping with their terror. They're not going to sit by and wait for us to exchange politely worded letters. We need, as I'm sure you heard from the Prime Minister, we need to get Haiti back to its people. So, colleagues, I'll just conclude by saying we've tried a different model here. We have countries that were willing to join us in that effort. We now have thousands of personnel pledged and the resources to support them. It's time to finish what we've started and get the Haitian people the security they need so that they can then have the foreign direct investment, the economic growth, the education, the healthcare, and the other pieces that the Haitian people rightly deserve. And I thank you.

Thank you, Ambassador, for that timely update and reminder of where we need to go. Very, very much appreciated. I now turn to the representative of El Salvador, Her Excellency Adriana Mira, the Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs.

Thank you, Ambassador. The crisis that's affecting Haiti is still very complex. More than 6.4 people require humanitarian assistance and close to 1.5 million are internally displaced. Half of them are boys and girls. So these figures confirm that humanitarian response is still indispensable, but it cannot be conceived as a permanent response. Institutional security and stability and development need to go in parallel and reinforce each other. For El Salvador, the progress made in the area of security should be consolidated. The recovery of the space against the gang should translate into an effective presence of the state, the establishment of basic services, more access to justice, and new opportunities for the community. The commitment of El Salvador towards Haiti has been shown through time from MINUSAS to the GSF. Our contingent is comprised of hundreds of Salvadoran soldiers. Our experience has shown that to regain this condition of security can open avenues of transformation, but this should be coupled with solid institutions, opportunities for the youth, and a sustained long-term vision. This advisory board has a particular value to connect this immediate response with cooperation for development in a way that's more predictable, coherent, and aligned with Haiti's priorities. In the context of the renewal of the GSF mandate, El Salvador calls to include an adequate regime in terms of privileges of the personnel so that we can comply with the forces mandate and overcome the weaknesses that have been identified. We need to have clear rules, a plan, a procedure, and less bureaucracy. El Salvador will continue to support Haiti at the United Nations and on the ground with a firm commitment with its security, stability, and development.
Thank you.
Thank you, Your Excellency.
Floor to the representative of Spain, Her Excellency Susana Sumelzo Jordan, Secretary of State for Ibero-American and Caribbean Affairs.

Muchas gracias, President.

Thank you, Mr. President. Many of us that took the floor and many others, we have had a meeting of foreign ministers of Ibero-American ministers, at the initiative of the Dominican Republic, we have all unanimously approved a common position of Ibero-American countries to support stability, security, and the sustainable development of Haiti. That's the first thing I wanted to stress. The entire Ibero-American nations are in support of Haiti. We're also here because we're aware of the worsening crisis in Haiti. which continues to face critical moments. And that effort of the international community, led by the United Nations, with the involvement of the OAS and CARICOM, have not yet succeeded in achieving a sustainable improvement in the situation. So we believe the creation of the GSF, with a large contingent of personnel on the ground, is undoubtedly a step forward. But efforts must be redoubled to ensure a swift and effective deployment, close collaboration with the Haitian police and armed forces, and actions that respect and guarantee human rights. Spain supports the ongoing efforts in the Security Council to renew and strengthen its mandate. Restoring security is indispensable to recover and have elections again, but we also must work in parallel to develop a long-term strategy that addresses the root causes of violence and inequality with a particular focus on disarmament, demobilization, and integration. so that Haiti's active participation in this entire process is indispensable. We're particularly concerned about arms smuggling, which originates almost entirely from abroad. So we should focus our efforts in preventing this. Spain remains steadfast in its commitment to Haiti. In addition, We've contributed 1 million euros to the OAS Peace and Stabilization Operations Programs. Our embassy has remained open, and we have tripled our humanitarian assistance in recent years, which now amounts to almost 12 million euros. You can count on our commitment to continue working in a coordinated manner to help Haiti overcome this critical situation as soon as possible so that it can move forward on the path of development, growth, and progress. Thank you.
Thank the representative from Spain and I now turn the floor to the representative from the Caribbean Community or CARICOM Secretariat, Dr. Carla Barnett, who is the Secretary General.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. Excellencies, the Organization of American States High-Level Inter-American and International Delegation Mission to Haiti in mid-August of this year, in which I participated as the representative of the Caribbean community, came away from Haiti with the clear conclusion that strong coordination and collective activity must remain at the forefront of our efforts to support the long-term stability and development of Haiti. Shortly after, the CARICOM Eminent Persons Group visited Haiti at the beginning of September to engage with political actors, including the new parties and coalitions, which are emerging to facilitate dialogue among the various stakeholders and interests involved in the electoral process. Both missions have provided us with updated information on the situation on the ground, including the progress made on the electoral preparations and addressing the security challenges. Some progress has been made by the Provisional Electoral Council with the implementation of the electoral decree and the publication of deadlines for the registration of voters and candidates ahead of the first round of elections currently scheduled for the 13th of December, 2026. However, challenges persist, which hinder the ability of persons to register to vote and of candidates to meet the requirements or approval to participate in the elections. Critically, it is very difficult for persons and candidates to safely move around the country as many of the main highways are controlled by the armed gangs. A minimum level of effective security must be achieved in order that persons can safely move around to participate in the upcoming elections, whether as voters or as candidates. The renewal of the GSF mandate is critical, as is the rapid deployment of troops at the level required. We urge the international partners to work in concert to ensure that troops have timely and adequate airlift, equipment, and resources to provide an increased security presence with urgency. Simultaneously, efforts to strengthen Haiti's justice systems must be redoubled to support the implementation of the disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration strategy. In this regard, we welcome the launch of the Multi-Partner Trust Fund. On the humanitarian front, we also commend the ongoing work by international partners to address growing health, food, education, and migration issues that beset the Haitian population. Excellencies, at the heart of the matter, the outlook for Haiti remains one in need of energized and harmonized international support. coordination has become a critical enabling factor to avoid duplication and to ensure that the pressing needs of the Haitian people are addressed. We must continue to work in solidarity and shared commitment with our regional and international partners in assisting the people and the institutions of Haiti to develop and implement solutions by Haiti, for Haiti, and of Haiti. The people of Haiti are counting on us to stand with them as they strive to move towards stability, democratic renewal, and long-term sustainable development. We must not let them down. I thank you very much.
Thank you. Thank you, Representative Karakom, for her statement. And I now turn to Turkey, His Excellency Zeki Lavant Gorunzu, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of Turkey.

And thanks to Canada for organizing this meeting and for their leadership in this group. In fact, I took the floor, but everything that I wanted to say has already been said and much more eloquently than I can ever do, so I decided not to repeat them. But I also realized in the meantime that we are one of the few countries from outside the region to attend this meeting and take the floor. So I thought it might be interesting to some maybe why a country like Turkey from thousands of kilometers away care that much for Haiti. So I wanted to clarify that for you. That's first and foremost because Based on our limited but very teaching experience, we know what Haitian people are capable of, what a big potential they have, and how much they deserve to benefit from the talent, resources, and opportunities existing in Haiti, as Prime Minister mentioned, in fact. And also, we know that a stable, secure, and prosperous Haiti is going to be a security provider in this region, rather than a security consumer. So we believe that our support to Haiti is In fact, I mean, an investment in not only in the future of Haiti, but in the future of this region, which is of course, indispensable for global security and politics. And secondly, because we see international security as indivisible. And we believe that even a crisis in a small country like Haiti will have an impact on other regions in all parts of the world. So that's why we believe that, I mean, we have to act. None of the countries in the world can stay indifferent to what's happening in Haiti and that we have to act with a sense of shared responsibility for our common security. So this is why, as Turkey, we have long contributed to UN's efforts to maintain and to restore security, either by our police forces or through financial and we will certainly continue doing that. And if I may, though, of course, our contributions to security is so valuable and must continue, either through GSF or other means. But they can by no means, of course, substitute in Haitian-led and Haitian-owned process. That is a must for sustainable stability, recovery, and long-term development, of course. And that can also be possible, of course, only through fair and credible elections and the establishment strong national institutions that will fight corruption, that will provide inequality, but that will also restore hope in the minds of the young Haitians for a future without gangs. And we will continue to support Haiti in that vitally important process as well. Thank you so much.
Thank you, Excellency, for that timely intervention. I now turn to the representative from Cuba. Her Excellency Anayansi Rodriguez Camejo, who is the Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs.

Thank you, Ambassador. Once again, we are gathered. We have the urgent need to address the multidimensional crisis that Haiti is facing, that continues to suffer the consequences of centuries of colonial and neocolonial exploitation and also foreign actions. Haiti requires a genuine response by the international community. Its people needs cooperation and solidarity. For decades, Cuba has provided our sister nation collaboration. Since 1998, our health cooperation staff has supported Haiti uninterruptedly. Currently, There is a brigade comprised of more than 50 Cubans, continuing to provide health services in the south of the country. Cuban solidarity has also extended to other areas for development in Haiti, such as education, culture, water resources, fisheries, and the environment. Cuba urges all governments and international organizations and donors to double their efforts to mobilize the financial resources that are necessary to facilitate technology transfer, promote capacity building nationally, and to honor the commitments and the aid for development for Haiti. All cooperation efforts must respond to the needs of the Haitian people. and should be conducted respecting their sovereignty, their independence, their government, their institution, and the right of their people to decide freely their own destiny. Thank you.

Colleagues, we're at time. I'm very sorry. We have a hard stop at noon, and I would like to give the Minister of Foreign Affairs the ability to finish. I would like to correct the record, and I apologize sincerely for countries who have come and who have supported the mission and who did not get a chance to speak. Again, sincerely apologize. I would like to correct the record before we turn the final conclusion over to the Minister of Foreign Affairs. The Secretary of State for Canada misspoke when he called pledging when he said, he should have said pleaders instead of countries, he said countries. And so he included an entity that was not a country in that list. And so I just want to correct the record. Thank you. Minister of Foreign Affairs.

Thank you. I apologize for those who cannot share their comments. I would really love to hear them, but I understand we're out of time. I would love to receive the statements, if you don't mind. Thank you so much. I will do my address in French.

Excellences, Mesdames, Messieurs.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. So Haiti presented its candidacy to for the 2027 elections. So I would like to reiterate the commitment to continue to show the progress of implementation of SDGs and to identify the gaps and the need, the humanitarian needs, especially when it comes to statistical needs and core and institutional coordination with the support and the help of UN organizations. In the honor of the Republic of Haiti, I'd like to express our sincere thanks to the ECOSOC Council of the UN to have dedicated this dialogue to Haiti's future and to have the interventions today have shown that we have shared beliefs, security, economic development, economic development and the government's development are not competing priorities, but are different dimensions of the same our project of nation rebuilding. There's no progress can be made if these pillars do not advance. Simultaneously, the prime minister shared his vision, a vision of Haiti that goes from a logic of assistance to a logic of innovation, job creation, and partnership. So this ambition is based on concrete perspectives of development and a resolve to work with regional and international partners. The Minister of Defence on his end reminded us that economic transformation cannot happen without a significant improvement of the security environment. The efforts that have been put into place to strengthen the capacity of the national defense to fight against illicit flows and to restore state authority needs to be accompanied by international cooperation. All these interventions show the same reality. Haiti is progressing with lucidity, with responsibility, and with determination. But the challenges are important, but they do not define our country necessarily. We want to reiterate our willingness to build stronger institutions, a more competitive economy, and a more resilient economy. Ladies and gentlemen, I just want to reiterate my gratitude to international organizations, member states who continue to accompany the state, the Haitian people, all the confidence that you have expressed towards Haiti that continue to give us precious support. The Haitian government will continue to create favorable conditions for credible, free and fair elections, considered to consolidate the rule of law and to restart the economy. So these goals are in line with the legitimate ambitions of the Haitian people. Ladies and gentlemen, this meeting is not the end of our dialogue, but an opening of our partnerships and the ideas that have been expressed today should now be translated into decisions. We ask our partners to continue to work with us because investing in Haiti's stability means investing in the stability of our region. strengthening the capacity of the Haitian state is to contribute to a more durable peace, more efficient cooperation, and more shared prosperity. The history will not remember the difficulties that we faced, but will retain the collective will that we've shown to overcome them. So let us make it so that this This meeting will be the result of a renewed will based on shared responsibilities. We should move forward with the same determination to reestablish security, to strengthen democratic order, disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration, as well as on the economic recovery. All these pillars are interdependent pillars of the same effort. None of these pillars can be successful alone. If we neglect one pillar, we weaken the others. This would compromise our capacity to find a sustainable way out of the Haitian crisis. To conclude, I say this with humility. wherever there is injustice, that there's a threat to justice everywhere. Today, Haiti reminds us that the dignity of our people cannot be... We in Haiti, we're defending all the values that we share together, peace, justice, human dignity. Today, Haiti is not just asking for solidarity. It is also asking for shared responsibility for security, for dignity, for development, and for the future of its people. Thank you.
